svg.text: KubeEdge: from kubectl to a LoRa board
What each hop is, in terms you already know from Kubernetes
THE MAPPING TO PLAIN KUBERNETES
CloudCore — runs in the cluster. Watches the API server and relays to edge nodes over one persistent WebSocket. It exists because an edge node cannot be assumed to reach the API server directly.
EdgeCore — runs on the edge box. Contains a trimmed kubelet (Edged), a local SQLite cache (MetaManager) so the node keeps working while disconnected, and DeviceTwin.
DeviceTwin — no Kubernetes analogue. A desired/reported state store for physical things. Think of it as status subresource semantics, but for hardware that is asleep half the time.
Mapper — your code. Closest analogue is a CSI driver or device plugin: a protocol-specific adapter registered with the node agent over gRPC. One mapper per protocol, not per device.
Everything below is the standard controller pattern — watch, diff, act, report — with a WebSocket tunnel and a device adapter bolted on the end.
PHASE 1 — NODE JOIN. One-time. This is the bit with no Kubernetes equivalent: a token exchange over a WebSocket instead of a kubelet bootstrap.
read join token from Secret
keadm gettoken
EdgeHub dials CloudHub :10000, presents token
keadm join — WebSocket, edge dials out, so no inbound firewall rule
issue client certs
token is single-use; certs are what the tunnel uses from here on
register Node object (proxied via CloudCore)
now `kubectl get nodes` shows the edge box — it looks like an ordinary node
PHASE 2 — MAPPER REGISTRATION (DMI). Like a CSI driver registering with the kubelet: gRPC over a unix socket, announcing which protocol it speaks.
RegisterMapper(protocol: "esphome")
gRPC on /etc/kubeedge/dmi.sock
here are the Devices on this node with protocol=esphome
served from MetaManager's local cache — works even if the cloud is unreachable
PHASE 3 — DEVICE CREATION. From here it is the ordinary controller pattern you already know, with two extra hops on the end.
apply Device
devices.kubeedge.io/v1beta1
watch event
DeviceController is an ordinary informer — nothing exotic here
device spec down the tunnel
routed by spec.nodeName — the same WebSocket opened in step 2
MetaManager persists to SQLite; DeviceTwin creates the twin
this is the edge-autonomy step — state survives a cloud outage or a reboot
DMI: device added
driver connects
MQTT subscribe to w10-a/#
PHASE 4 — REPORTED STATE FLOWS UP. Temperature leaves the board and ends up in Device.status. This is your V0 milestone.
MQTT: temperature = 26.8
ESPHome publishes on its own schedule; the mapper does not poll
DMI: ReportDeviceStatus
normalised into twin properties by the framework, not by you
DeviceTwin updates the reported value
if the cloud link is down it stops here and syncs later — nothing is lost
status up the tunnel
PATCH Device.status.twins
ordinary status subresource write
kubectl get device w10-a
V0 IS DONE HERE. A number measured by an SHT41 on your desk is now readable with kubectl.
Everything after this — writes, OTA, canary rollouts, LoRa awareness — is addition, not architecture.
PHASE 5 — DESIRED STATE FLOWS DOWN. V1. The same path in reverse, and where the sleepy-node problem actually lives.
patch desired
tx_enable = "ON"
watch event
desired twin down the tunnel
DMI: UpdateDevTwins
WriteDevice → MQTT publish
device confirms new state
reported catches up with desired — the loop closes
WHERE THE KUBERNETES ANALOGY STRAINS — the three things worth designing for before writing code
Reconcile latency. controller-runtime assumes requeue-in-seconds. A LoRa node asleep 95% of the time wants requeue-on-next-contact. "Pending until the device next wakes" has to be
a first-class state, not a retry loop. This is why the mapper holds intent on the device's behalf rather than the controller retrying — the gateway is the kubelet, the device is the workload.
Intent staleness. A node offline for a week wakes to three queued generations of desired state. Collapse to latest, or apply in order? Kubernetes never has to answer this because
a pod that misses an update is simply recreated. A physical device cannot be recreated.
Partial reachability. A device that exists, is healthy, and is merely unreachable right now. Kubernetes calls that NotReady and evicts. You must not. KubeEdge's edge-autonomy
design already assumes this, which is the single strongest reason to build on it rather than rolling your own controller.
None of these block V0. They decide whether V2 is sound.
Steps 1–6 are one-time setup. Steps 7–18 are the read path and your first milestone. Steps 19–24 are the write path.
Only steps 12, 13, 14 and 23 are code you write. Everything else is KubeEdge.
